body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: Our bustling dramatists having run through all their varieties of comedy, farce, opera, interlude, melo-drama, and pantomime, and being at last fairly put to a nonplus, have suddenly bethought themselves, in spite of the ridicule of the spectators and the exhaustion of their poor beasts, of beginning the race over again,—hardened, it seems, against the innumerable thumps, kicks, and falls they have received by the way, and careless what figure they may cut provided when they pull off their hats at the conclusion, the crowd take pity on them and clap their backs. The animals however on which these kind of races are performed, are of a nature exceedingly stubborn; and though their riders, in the present instance, have done all they could to flatter and edge them on,—endeavouring to hide the length of their ears with all sorts of fine ribbons, and digging them every instant with their pointless heels, the creatures positively refuse to go back the whole length of the course; they stare; they prick up their ears; they plant their legs against procedure; they are frightened at the laughter and tumult which await them at the place of starting; in short, it is impossible to get them farther than melo-drama; and even there they would do nothing were it not for certain foreigners in the crowd,—German and French,—who being flattered by the riders' applications, and accustomed in their own countries to the management of such palfreys, kindly lend their assistance and ingenuity to effect a movement, till at last the poor (I wish I could say, dumb) animals come in again with such waving of penny flags and blowing of penny trumpets, and such pathetic efforts on the part of the said Germans, that the little boys who are present cannot contain their admiration and almost begin to envy them. It is true, there was an attempt the other day, on the part of an experienced rider named Dibdin, to commence at the old place; and by keeping his beast out of sight a little and bringing it round through the bye-lanes, he certainly did contrive to appear again at the starting post; but his hack got a dreadful fall, and he was taken up for dead.

Allegory apart, however, the dramatists are really reduced to the nonplus abovementioned; and after the complete failure of Mr. Dibdin's comedy, it is not likely that they will endeavour to return to their old, original sins. Accordingly, the whole set of them, old and young, have lately taken to translation from such German or French dramas as are a little above the pitch of their own productions, a practice, which was well enough when used in moderation and out of a real modesty in the translator, but not to be endured as a mere refuge for idle or exhausted nonsense, especially when it threatens us with a revival of maudlin German pieces, which have been read and ridiculed without end, and long been given up by the better taste of the public. Yet this is the present state of the British drama. Mr. Hook gives us his little pieces from the French; Mr. Pocock gives us his little pieces; Mr. Dimond gives us his little pieces; and Mr. Reynolds has recourse to translations already made, in order to give us his little pieces. At length, there seems to have been a dearth of new originals; when Mr. Charles Kemble, unluckily betaking himself to the set of German Plays translated by Mr. Thompson, and presenting us with a new Count Benyowski, reminds Mr. Reynolds of the existence of that ancient treasure, and accordingly, out of the same author and from the very same volume (German Theatre, Vol. III.) comes the Virgin of the Sun, which is now performing in the most splendid manner and, of course, with the greatest applause, on the "classical stage" of Covent-Garden.

This play by Kotzebue,—for it is a mere transcript from the German Theatre, with the addition of such vulgarisms and common-place as Mr. Reynolds thought himself bound to supply,—is a sort of companion to Pizarro, and contains the early part of the history of Rolla, who is here first made acquainted with Cora's passion for Alonzo, and devotes himself with a romantic philosophy to their future happiness, and finally saves them from the punishment of the vestal law which they had violated, and of which he accomplishes the abolition. There is unquestionably something very elevating in the contemplation of Rolla's character; and it has never been denied that the German dramatists possess a feeling for the pathetic and impassioned,—sometimes even for the sublime; but the feeling is so deluged with affectation,—there is such a morbid preference about them, of high-wrought sensibilities and maddening provocatives to the solid comforts within our reach,—such a nonsensical and dangerous reliance on impressions instead of principles,—such grave attempts to exalt the babbling of everyday feelings into something new and surprising,—such badness of taste, such lachrymose imposture, such beggarly egotism;—in a word, such cant of every description, that they have no more pretence, or rather just about as much pretence, to stand in the same rank with true and triumphant genius, as the ravings of a diseased idleness have to be accounted oracles of wisdom, or the Lectures of Mr. Coleridge to render him worthy of the Poets he pretends to analyze. I shall therefore be excused from repeating all that has been said in conviction of these German offenders and of their unfortunate aiders and abettors nor will it be necessary to enter into any further account of the Piece before us, the reader will easily conceive the expense that is thrown away upon it in dresses and decorations,—the flags, the frankincense, and the processions; and he will lament, as usual, the want of rival and well-sized Theatres, that might relieve us from this stupendous booth.

The music by Mr. Bishop evinces his usual science; and in the full instrumental parts is highly expressive and imposing; but he does not appear to have advanced in point of invention. The sweet voice and delicate taste of Mr. Sinclair are not heard to advantage in the noisy parts that are given him; but then, to make us amends perhaps, the voice of Miss Feron is heard too much. This young lady has some taste and more power of lungs, and seems to have been injudiciously encouraged in exerting a voice, which is by no means pleasanter when it is loudest. Some of the upper tones are a singular mixture of mellowness and harshness; and the middle ones degenerate into a sort of splay-footed jollity, like those of Master Smalley. With a little less manifest reliance on her powers of pleasing, and the instructions of some abler advisers than those who seem to have been about her,—Miss Feron will probably become a very tolerable actress and agreeable singer.

The soundest part of the whole entertainment is afforded by Mr. Young's performance of Rolla, which is the very best of it's kind on the stage. His emphasis on pronouncing the reluctant word "brother," when he resolves to forego his own feelings and embraces his Cora's husband, is extremely touching and full of meaning; and so is every situation in which he finds himself in her presence. His performance indeed, throughout, exhibits a true conception of his character,—that is to say, a vehement but equable glow of heart and highmindedness, alike removed from the sophisticated parade of Mr. Kemble and the boyish extravagance of Pope. Mr. Young feels warmly, and when he takes pains to do it, can think as justly. If he would cease to be content with being merely good in general, and set himself ambitiously to study every new and important character he has to perform, Mr. Kemble's present superiority, I think, would vanish before him.
